stem:
An 11-month-old boy has had 30 hours of intermittent screaming with pallor and drawing up of his legs, and has vomited twice. He passed a small redcurrant-jelly stool this morning. Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic intussusception with a small amount of free fluid. After a 10 mL/kg saline bolus he is pink with a heart rate of 130/min, a soft abdomen and no peritonism.

What is the most appropriate next step, decided with the surgical team?

options.label: A
options.text: Laparotomy, as the bloody stool indicates ischaemic bowel
options.explanation: Redcurrant-jelly stool reflects mucosal congestion and is common. It is not a contraindication to enema reduction in a stable child without peritonism.

options.label: B
options.text: Laparotomy, as symptoms have lasted more than 24 hours
options.explanation: A longer history lowers the success rate but is not by itself a contraindication; a stable child should still have an attempt at enema reduction.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 6 hours to allow spontaneous reduction
options.explanation: Transient small-bowel intussusceptions often reduce by themselves, but a symptomatic ileocolic intussusception needs reduction now.

options.label: D
options.text: IV antibiotics, nasogastric drainage and observation
options.explanation: Supportive care alone leaves the intussusception unreduced and risks bowel ischaemia.

options.label: E
options.text: Air enema reduction with the surgical team available
options.explanation: Correct. He is resuscitated with no peritonitis or perforation, so image-guided air enema reduction with surgeons available is first line, despite the bloody stool, free fluid and 30-hour history.

context: Stable ileocolic intussusception is reduced by air enema with surgeons available. Peritonitis, perforation and shock that does not respond to fluids are contraindications; bloody stool, a small amount of free fluid and a longer history are not.
